planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to occasionally wet soil in full sun to partial shade; give it a small-footprint spot since it stays far more compact than a typical vernal witch hazel.

directions: Quasimodo is a true dwarf selection of the native Ozark witch hazel, discovered by Dutch nurseryman Pieter Zwijnenburg and introduced into the European trade around 1980. It stays only 30 to 40 inches tall and wide even after many years, keeping the species' spicy-sweet, ribbon-petaled light orange flowers and vase-shaped habit in a scale suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, or large containers. New growth has a soft blue-green cast that holds up well through summer before turning a respectable yellow in autumn. Site it in acidic, well-drained to occasionally wet soil in full sun or light shade and expect a slow-growing, long-lived shrub that needs minimal pruning.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; registered by McDaniel in 1971 for its unusually early, long-lasting bloom.

directions: Christmas Cheer is a very early-flowering selection of the native Ozark witch hazel, opening its small, citrus-scented, strap-petaled flowers around the winter solstice and continuing to bloom for roughly ten weeks into late winter, well ahead of most other vernal witch hazel selections. Each flower pairs a crimson calyx with golden-yellow petals, giving a warm two-tone glow against bare branches on mild winter days. Summer foliage is clean green, turning a consistent clear butter-yellow in fall. Grow in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune only lightly after flowering to maintain its rounded, multi-stemmed form.

common_name: New Year Gold Vernal Witch Hazel

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; another McDaniel selection noted for flowering ahead of nearly all other vernal witch hazel cultivars.

directions: New Year Gold produces clear, solid golden-yellow, ribbon-like flowers that open as early as any vernal witch hazel selection, often starting around the turn of the new year on mild days and holding well through cold spells. The sweetly fragrant blooms appear on bare stems ahead of the foliage, which emerges green in spring and turns gold to orange in autumn. Grow this upright, multi-stemmed native shrub in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade along a streambank or woodland edge, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; described by Edwards in 1997 for its dark-calyxed, bright orange flowers.

directions: Orange Spangles carries a dark maroon-red calyx behind bright yellow-orange, strap-shaped petals, giving the late-winter flower display unusually strong contrast compared to the more uniformly colored vernal witch hazel cultivars. It is a vigorous grower, capable of reaching 8 to 10 feet within its first decade, and like other selections of the species carries a sweet, spicy fragrance on the bare-branch flowers. Fall foliage turns gold to orange. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it enough room to mature into a large, upright, multi-stemmed shrub.
sources: Witch Hazel Nursery National Plant Collection

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; introduced by Girard Nurseries of Ohio around 1980.

directions: Girard's Orange bears thin, twisted petals that shift from yellow at the tips to a deeper orange near the base of the flower, opening at the very first mild spell of late winter and holding on through subsequent cold snaps. It makes a wide, spreading rather than strictly upright shrub, and tolerates a broad range of soils and light exposures provided the ground stays reasonably moist and it is sheltered from drying winter wind. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune lightly right after flowering to maintain an open, well-spaced branch structure.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; grown chiefly for variegated foliage rather than flower color.

directions: Green Thumb is a variegated sport of common witch hazel, with obovate leaves that open in spring showing an irregular dark green center surrounded by a paler green to chartreuse margin, a pattern that holds through the growing season rather than fading to plain green by summer. It still produces the species' typical small, fragrant, spidery yellow flowers directly on bare branches in fall, though the foliage pattern is the main selling point. Left to grow naturally it becomes a large, multi-stemmed understory shrub to small tree reaching 12 to 15 feet in a decade. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a genuine dwarf form of common witch hazel suited to smaller gardens.

directions: Little Suzie is a compact selection of common witch hazel that stays only 4 to 5 feet tall and wide after a decade, far smaller than the species' usual large-shrub scale, making it one of the few common witch hazels suited to a small foundation planting or mixed shrub border. It carries the species' characteristic long-petaled, highly fragrant yellow flowers, frequently opening in late fall while the clear yellow autumn foliage is still clinging to the stems, for a brief overlap of bloom and leaf color. Grow in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and expect a dense, rounded habit that needs little pruning to stay tidy.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a brightly variegated foliage selection of common witch hazel.

directions: Lemon Lime is grown for its boldly variegated foliage, with leaves irregularly splashed in yellow over the base green, giving the whole shrub a bright, two-tone look through the growing season well before the species' typical gold fall color sets in. It flowers like the straight species, with small, fragrant, spidery yellow blooms appearing on bare branches in fall, though the show of variegated leaves is the main reason to grow this selection. Reaching roughly 10 feet tall and wide at maturity, it works well as a large accent shrub at a woodland edge. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and prune only lightly to remove dead wood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; patented selection (US Plant Patent PP12100) found by breeder William Flemer III as a chance seedling.

directions: November Glow was discovered as a chance seedling by nurseryman William Flemer III in New Jersey and is notable for flowers roughly two and a half times larger than typical common witch hazel blooms, in a bright, clean yellow with pale orange-yellow stamens, opening in dense clusters on slender branches around the first half of November. New foliage emerges olive-green and matures to a yellowish green beneath, turning a strong orange-yellow in fall. It grows into a vigorous, upright, spreading shrub reaching roughly 7 to 8 feet tall and wide at maturity. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches since it resents heavy cutting back.
sources: US Plant Patent PP12100 (Hamamelis virginiana 'November Glow')
